primitives.name: Kinematic Snap
primitives.verbatim_quote: It is not the force that is put into the whole motion of the kick that will give it distance, but the snap that is put into the leg at the moment it strikes the ball.
primitives.assumptions: Contact impulse dominates distance; linear momentum transfer is instantaneous.
primitives.breakdown_regime: v_s → 0 implies zero distance; F_s → ∞ causes injury or loss of control.

layer2.mapping: Snap velocity v_s derived from F_s/t_c via impulse-momentum theorem; GSI models v_s as latent variable in Bayesian kick distance prediction.
layer2.telemetry: Ball trajectory deviation from intended arc

primitives.name: Step Precision
primitives.verbatim_quote: The steps taken just before the ball is kicked must not carry the kicker much forward toward the center.
primitives.assumptions: Forward step displacement must remain orthogonal to goal vector.
primitives.breakdown_regime: θ > π/2 implies collision with own line; L < 0 blocks opponent access.

layer2.mapping: Step geometry θ ≡ 0 maps to optimal kickoff alignment; GSE encodes step constraint as state transition boundary.
layer2.telemetry: Distance from center of field at contact point

primitives.name: Place Kick Form
primitives.verbatim_quote: PLACE KICK The place kick is made by placing the ball in position on the ground and kicking it from this location.
primitives.assumptions: Static placement allows precise angular control.
primitives.breakdown_regime: h_b → 0 implies ground contact; θ_d → π/2 implies misalignment.

layer2.mapping: Placement x_p defines initial condition for trajectory; GSI treats h_b as variance parameter in probabilistic kick model.

This aligns with Newtonian mechanics where momentum transfer at contact is paramount. The step precision primitive introduces geometric constraints—forward steps must not exceed a threshold to avoid positional disadvantage. These constraints define a bounded phase space for valid kicks. The place kick form establishes a foundational configuration where static placement enables deterministic control over direction and elevation. Together, these primitives form a minimal set of operators governing kick execution. Failure modes include insufficient snap leading to low velocity, excessive forward steps causing blocking vulnerability, and improper placement resulting in directional drift. Each operator exhibits a dual nature: snap governs magnitude, while step and placement govern orientation. The interplay between these three forms a closed-loop system where each component influences the others, forming an emergent tactical behavior.
